nameStory: The name 'devil's trumpet' comes from the plant's large, trumpet-shaped flowers that bloom at night, combined with its highly toxic and hallucinogenic properties that have long been associated with dark magic and dangerous rituals. The species name 'metel' comes from an ancient Sanskrit word 'dhatūra,' which is also the source of the genus name Datura, reflecting this plant's deep historical roots in Indian traditional medicine and spiritual practices.
description: Metel devil's trumpet is a bushy annual plant (or short-lived perennial in warmer areas) that grows 3-5 feet tall and wide. It produces spectacular large, white trumpet-shaped flowers that can be 6-8 inches long and face upward or outward from the plant. The flowers are followed by spiny, egg-shaped seed pods that split open to reveal dark seeds. This is an extremely poisonous plant in the nightshade family that should never be touched or consumed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large white trumpet-shaped flowers, 6-8 inches long, that point upward or outward (not downward). They have a sweet, intoxicating fragrance and typically open in the evening, staying open through the night and into the morning.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round to egg-shaped seed capsules covered in short, blunt spines that feel prickly but not dangerously sharp. The capsules split into four sections when ripe, revealing numerous dark brown or black seeds inside.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large oval leaves with pointed tips and smooth or slightly wavy edges. They feel soft and somewhat velvety to the touch, and are arranged alternately along the stems rather than in pairs.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a bushy, rounded shrub-like plant that branches extensively. The whole plant has a slightly fuzzy appearance and gives off a rank, unpleasant odor when leaves are crushed or bruised.

habitat: In New England, metel devil's trumpet is primarily found as an escaped garden plant in disturbed soils around old homesteads, abandoned gardens, and waste areas. It prefers warm, sheltered locations with rich, well-drained soil and is most likely to persist in southern New England's milder microclimates. This heat-loving plant struggles in New England's climate and is quite rare in the wild here.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate late in spring when soil warms up. Young plants emerge as small bushy seedlings with the characteristic soft, oval leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with spectacular trumpet flowers opening nightly. The sweet evening fragrance is most noticeable during warm, humid summer nights.
seasonality.fall: Spiny seed capsules mature and split open, releasing seeds. Plants may continue blooming until the first hard frost kills them.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely with frost. Only seeds survive winter, and germination success varies greatly depending on winter severity.

funFact: The flowers are essentially nocturnal party animals - they open in the evening with an intoxicating sweet perfume that can be smelled from 20 feet away, specifically to attract night-flying moths as pollinators, then often close or fade by the next afternoon!
confusionNotes: Often confused with angel's trumpets (Brugmansia species), but angel's trumpets have flowers that hang downward like bells, while devil's trumpet flowers point upward or outward like, well, trumpets! Remember: angels look down from heaven, devils point up from below.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'devil's trumpet,' this plant is sometimes confusingly also called 'angel's trumpet' in casual conversation, though true angel's trumpets are a different genus (Brugmansia). All parts of this plant contain dangerous tropane alkaloids that have caused serious poisonings and deaths, so it should be admired from a distance only.
compareHints: Metel devil's trumpet has larger, more ornamental upward-facing flowers compared to its weedy cousin jimsonweed, which has smaller white or purple flowers and more deeply toothed leaves. While jimsonweed is a common roadside weed throughout New England, metel is much rarer and typically only found where it was once cultivated as a garden ornamental.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Jimsonweed is the most common Datura species in New England, distinguished from its relatives by its upward-facing white flowers and especially spiny seed pods.

Sacred datura differs from its relative jimsonweed (the only other Datura commonly found in New England) by having much larger flowers, gray-green fuzzy leaves instead of bright green smooth ones, and a perennial growth habit rather than being an annual.
Unlike its cousin jimsonweed which has smooth leaves and upright white flowers, downy thorn-apple has that distinctive fuzzy texture and flowers that nod slightly downward.
